beats.say: Right now, your head is ageing faster than your feet. Not by much. But it is.
In October twenty twenty six, labs in Vienna and Beijing built the first clocks that tick with the centre of an atom.
To see why that matters, follow three clocks.
Clock one. The sea, seventeen oh seven. You're a navigator in bad weather. You can't tell how far east or west you've sailed. For that, you need the exact time.
That night, four British warships hit the rocks off the Scilly Isles. More than fourteen hundred sailors drowned.
Clock two. Your pocket, today. Your phone finds you by listening to satellites that carry atomic clocks.
Light moves thirty centimetres in a billionth of a second. Slip that much, and your dot is thirty centimetres off.
Clock three. A lab, October twenty twenty six. A laser shines on a crystal holding thorium atoms.
Here's the rule behind all three. A clock is only as good as the thing that ticks inside it.
In seventeen sixty one, John Harrison's sea clock lost just five seconds in eighty one days. Sailors finally knew where they were.
Atomic clocks count the caesium atom. Nine billion ticks a second. That's what keeps your dot on the map.
But they listen to the atom's electrons, and electrons get pushed around by heat and magnets.
So the new clocks listen deeper, to the nucleus, hidden behind its electrons. It ticks about two thousand trillion times a second.
Two separate teams, both published in Nature. The catch: they're not yet better than today's best atomic clocks. Vienna's team says they could get around ten thousand times steadier.
Clocks this good can feel gravity. In twenty twenty two, scientists caught time running faster just one millimetre higher.
So yes, your head is older than your feet. By about half a millionth of a second, over a lifetime.
